section: Sections 0–4 — the evidence rule, the commit table, the 90-second version, the adversary model, the five checkpoints, §3.2 the order of checks, §3.3 COVERAGE HONESTLY, and the four walkthroughs in §4

claims.claim: "Exactly one control in this product currently carries this label."
claims.evidence: Installers/internal/liveproof/register.json at origin/main (5b129523) holds 8 proof objects, of which THREE have observed:true — `pretooluse-deny-stops-side-effect` (2026-08-26T17:11:57Z), `signed-bundle-activates-and-digest-reaches-backend` (2026-08-27T10:50:01Z, commit c25aaa92), and `codex-hook-fires-and-client-honours-deny` (2026-08-27T11:48:30Z, commit 21ce3cc3). Five remain quarantined.
claims.correctedText: | **PROVEN LIVE** | Someone observed it work on a real machine and recorded the evidence. **Three of the eight controls in the live-proof register currently carry this label.** See §15.

claims.correctedText: the working checkouts on developer machines in this workspace are between five hundred and a thousand commits behind (measured 2026-08-28: Installers 1,010, Backend 773, Frontend 525)

claims.evidence: `git rev-parse origin/main` in Frontend = cac574ae063b4e91ec38ddb205ec5abe4cbc3dff ("Merge PR #188 fix/vendored-engine-refresh", 2026-08-27T01:41:22+03:00). Still the tip; nothing has landed on Frontend main since the document was written.

claims.claim: "Claude Code on a Windows endpoint is comprehensively governed"
claims.evidence: The register's own `hook-lane-prompt-block` entry (register.json, quarantine reason) records 10 identical private-key prompt runs at the shipped 60-second hook timeout: 4 blocked with 0 requests to the model, 6 NOT blocked with the private-key bytes egressing. ~/.devoid/undecidable-hook-payloads.json recorded {"total":11,"byReason":{"daemon-unreachable-budget-expired":11}} over the same 20-minute window. The lane is comprehensively WIRED; it is not comprehensively governing under load.
claims.correctedText: Claude Code on a Windows endpoint is comprehensively wired — every checkpoint, the wire, and the launch — and it is the only lane measured failing open under ordinary machine load (§15.1: six of ten runs leaked)

claims.claim: "Codex is governed at the machine layer while its cooperative hook lane is inert on current client versions"
claims.evidence: Installers/internal/codexmanaged/hookdialect.go:166 — `knownHookTrustDialects = []hookTrustDialect{hookTrustDialect144, hookTrustDialect147}`, two rows (prefixes "0.144." at :103 and "0.147." at :114). The 0.147 row was added on measurement, not assumption: hookdialect.go:120-160 records a 9-vector oracle corpus read back from the client's own `currentHash`, plus a live `codex exec` trust negative control. Register entry `codex-hook-fires-and-client-honours-deny` is observed:true — codex-cli 0.147.0 dispatched the PreToolUse hook, DeVoid returned block for a curl-pipe-to-shell, and the client refused the tool.
claims.correctedText: Codex is governed at the machine layer, and its cooperative hook lane now fires on the two client families whose trust format has been measured (0.144.x and 0.147.x) — proven live on 0.147 — while staying inert on every other build and on any endpoint carrying the machine baseline
claims.labelChange: INERT -> CONDITIONAL (condition: client version in {0.144.x, 0.147.x} AND no machine baseline pinning allow_managed_hooks_only). PROVEN LIVE on 0.147 cooperative scope, per register entry codex-hook-fires-and-client-honours-deny.

claims.claim: "the defaults lean toward *telling you* rather than *stopping you*"
claims.evidence: Backend/src/ai-security-policy/ai-security-policy.constants.ts:1423 — `AI_TOOL_RISK_DEFAULT_ACTIONS = resolveToolRiskDefaults(AI_TOOL_RISK_CLASSES, AI_TOOL_RISK_D4_TIERS, AI_MALICIOUS_FLOOR)`. The file's own docblock at :1199 states the shipped tally: **23 block / 2 warn / 12 monitor / 3 allow**, not the D4 table's 15/6/16/3. 23 of 40 tool-risk classes stop the developer by default, and the 23 malicious-floor toolRisk members (ai-malicious-floor.ts:143-183) cannot be relaxed below block by any administrator now that withMaliciousFloorApplied is the first statement of assembleEffectiveDto (ai-security-policy.service.ts:2198).
claims.correctedText: That assumption shapes the *detectors*: they report far more than they stop. It no longer shapes the *defaults*. Twenty-three of the forty behavioural classes block on the shipped default, and thirty-nine classes across tool-risk, DLP and prompt-risk sit on a malicious floor that a customer's administrator cannot relax — the console will accept the change, store it, and serve the floored value anyway.

claims.claim: "a fail-closed checkpoint on an unprovable condition made a machine unusable in July 2026 and the operator removed the agent"
claims.evidence: Installers commit 444afe5a (2026-07-31T03:04:18+03:00), "fix(ai-hooks): a dead daemon must not deny every tool call": "An unreachable daemon made EVERY hook checkpoint deny... on 2026-07-31 an operator uninstalled the agent to get their machine back." The mechanism is named: INTERVENTION_UNAVAILABLE was routed to the failure oracle and denied; it is now resolved to proceed in cmd/devoid/ai_failure_resolver.go:81 and internal/airuntime/runner.go:933.

claims.claim: "refuse to start it; force its traffic through us; strip bypass flags"
claims.evidence: cmd/devoid/agent_shim.go runAgentShim: refusal at the surface gate, provider deny-list and governance (three `return 1` paths); transport injection at step 5 via buildAgentEnv/enforceManagedTransportRoute; flag strip at step 5b via enforceGovernanceBypassFlags. All three exist. BUT each is narrower than the row implies: TransportEnvFor (internal/aiagent/aiagent.go:~128) returns proxied=true only for claude-code, false for codex, and ("", false) for gemini — so this checkpoint forces NO traffic for Codex or Gemini; and claudeGovernanceBypassFlags (agent_shim.go) is a one-element list `{"--bare"}` applied only when normalized=="claude", and on a COOPERATIVE endpoint the flag is honoured rather than stripped (enforceGovernanceBypassFlags, `if !managed { … return args }`).
claims.correctedText: | 1 | **The launch** — we replace `claude` / `codex` / `gemini` on PATH | that an agent is starting, and with what flags | refuse to start it; force **Claude's** traffic through us (Codex is routed by a persisted config entry instead, Gemini not at all); strip **Claude's** one known bypass flag `--bare`, and only on a managed endpoint — a cooperative endpoint honours it and merely records the attempt |

claims.claim: "Claude Code and Codex call out to a program before acting… deny the prompt, deny the tool call, replace the tool result"
claims.evidence: internal/airuntime/adapters/ contains exactly two directories, claudecode and codex (`git ls-tree -d origin/main internal/airuntime/adapters/`). Claude effects: internal/airuntime/adapters/claudecode/detect.go:29-33 (DenyPrompt, DenyTool, ReplaceOutput, None, None). Codex effects: internal/airuntime/adapters/codex/effects.go:44-50 (deny-prompt, deny-tool, replace-tool-result-with-feedback-and-continue, deny-escalation, none).

claims.claim: "the daemon watching configs, plugins, MCP servers, extensions… quarantine a plugin or MCP server; report drift"
claims.evidence: internal/mcpsources/mcpsources.go defines 16 discovery sources across 12 distinct ClientIDs (claude-code ×2, claude-desktop, codex ×2, cursor ×2, windsurf, gemini-cli, claude-code-state, vscode ×2, vscode-insiders, vscodium, cursor-app, windsurf-app). internal/extwatch/watcher.go and internal/browserinv/browserinv.go carry the extension lane; internal/plugingate/ the plugin lane.

claims.claim: "Where lanes overlap, they combine **most-restrictive-wins**."
claims.evidence: internal/daemon/ai_handlers.go:2759-2762 (`mergeToolDecision` — "Neither scanner can relax the other"), :2768 and :2791 (`foldArtifactDecision` / plugin fold — "can only ever TIGHTEN"), internal/daemon/ai_skill_verdict.go:235. In the browser lane the same posture appears as "the daemon… can only *upgrade* the verdict" (§5.4). NOTE the precision gap: every one of these folds is INSIDE one checkpoint's decision. There is no combiner that folds the hook lane's verdict with the wire lane's or the browser lane's — those overlap only in the weaker sense that either can independently refuse.
claims.correctedText: Where detectors overlap inside one checkpoint they combine **most-restrictive-wins**, and the code says so: neither the behaviour scanner nor the content scanner can relax the other, and an artifact or plugin verdict can only tighten. Across *lanes* there is no combiner: a prompt that traverses both the hook and the wire is decided twice, independently, and the strict outcome wins only because either lane can refuse on its own. Nothing reconciles a hook allow with a wire block, or records that the two disagreed.

claims.claim: "**Surface Access** — a five-row allow/monitor/block matrix over browser sites, CLI agents, IDE, third-party browser extensions and MCP"
claims.evidence: Backend/src/ai-security-policy/ai-security-policy.constants.ts:583-589 — `AI_SURFACE_KEYS = ['browser','cliAgents','ide','browserExtensions','mcp']`, exactly five. :573 — `AI_SURFACE_ACCESS_MODES = ['allow','monitor','block']`, exactly three.

claims.claim: "is evaluated *first*, before any detector runs"
claims.evidence: True on the shim and on both prompt lanes, false on the tool lane. internal/daemon/ai_handlers.go:2701 runs `findings := toolrisk.Scan(body.ToolName, body.ToolInput)` — the behavioural detector — as step 1; the surface gate `gv := evaluateAIGovernance(policy, body.AgentType, toolSurface)` is step 2a at :2717, sixteen lines later. By contrast the prompt lanes do put the gate first (:1245 and :2600 both precede their `dlp.ScanAll` at :2423 and :2630). The consequence is bounded — the surface short-circuit at :2718 returns `Findings: []` so nothing leaks — but the claim as written is not what the tool lane does.
claims.correctedText: A coarse gate outranks every fine one. **Surface Access** — a five-row allow/monitor/block matrix over browser sites, CLI agents, IDE, third-party browser extensions and MCP — is evaluated before any *decision* is composed. It is literally first on the shim and on both prompt lanes; on the tool lane the behavioural scan runs sixteen lines ahead of it (`ai_handlers.go:2701` vs `:2717`), so the gate short-circuits the decision but not the work, and the short-circuit response deliberately carries an empty findings array.

claims.claim: "If an administrator sets `cliAgents: block`, the shim prints a refusal and returns before it even locates the real binary."
claims.evidence: cmd/devoid/agent_shim.go runAgentShim: the surface switch (`case aiagent.SurfaceModeBlock: … return 1`) sits between step 1 (policy fetch) and step 2 (provider deny-list); `resolveRealAgentBinary` is step 4, strictly after. agentShimSurfaceMode reads `policy.Surfaces.CliAgents` through `aiagent.NormalizeSurfaceMode`.

claims.claim: "**SHIPS**; the default for every row is `allow`."
claims.evidence: Backend ai-security-policy.constants.ts:600 — `AI_SURFACE_ACCESS_DEFAULT: AiSurfaceAccessMode = 'allow'`, with the docblock "absent section, absent key, null, typo, or an injected token this runtime does not recognise". Endpoint side: internal/aiagent/aiagent.go:58-67 `NormalizeSurfaceMode` — `default: return SurfaceModeAllow`. Label SHIPS holds; but the gate is skipped entirely, not merely defaulted, when `policyOK` is false (agent_shim.go `agentShimSurfaceMode` returns allow if `!policyOK || policy == nil || policy.Surfaces == nil`).
claims.correctedText: **SHIPS**; the default for every row is `allow` — and so is the *absence* of a policy. A shim that could not fetch a policy at all does not apply the surface gate, it allows: `agentShimSurfaceMode` returns `allow` whenever the fetch failed, the policy is nil, or the surfaces section is absent.

claims.docLine: L135 (§3.3, Claude Code CLI row — Hooks column)
claims.claim: "5 events, 2 can deny"
claims.evidence: internal/aihooks/settings.go:134 — `var managedEvents = []string{evUserPromptSubmit, evPreToolUse, evPostToolUse, evSessionStart, evSessionEnd}` — five. internal/airuntime/adapters/claudecode/detect.go:29-33 — only UserPromptSubmit (EffectDenyPrompt) and PreToolUse (EffectDenyTool) carry a deny; PostToolUse is EffectReplaceOutput, SessionStart/SessionEnd are EffectNone.

claims.docLine: L135 (§3.3, Claude Code CLI row — Wire column)
claims.claim: "yes (`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` injected)"
claims.evidence: internal/aiagent/aiagent.go TransportEnvFor: `case AgentTypeClaude: return "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL", true`. cmd/devoid/agent_shim.go agentProxyBaseURL() = daemonBaseURL()+"/proxy/anthropic". internal/aihooks/transport_route.go:31,38,45 pins the same key, subtree and default port 19280 so the terminal and IDE launches route identically.

claims.docLine: L135 (§3.3, Claude Code CLI row — Verdict)
claims.claim: "**Fully covered.** The reference lane."
claims.evidence: This is the one row a reader will quote, and it is the row §15.1 disproves. register.json `hook-lane-prompt-block`: at the shipped 60-second timeout, 6 of 10 identical private-key runs proceeded unchecked and the key egressed; the mechanism was DeVoid's own budget expiry (`daemon-unreachable-budget-expired`, 11 occurrences), not the client. A verdict cell that says "fully covered" beside a measured 60% leak rate is the most damaging single string in the document.
claims.correctedText: | **Claude Code (CLI)** | yes | 5 events, 2 can deny | yes (`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` injected) | n/a | **Every lane wired — and the only lane measured leaking.** The reference implementation; six of ten private-key prompts egressed under load (§15.1). |
claims.labelChange: Fully covered -> CONDITIONAL (condition: the daemon answers inside the 4-second decision budget; under load it does not)

claims.docLine: L136 (§3.3, Claude in an IDE / Desktop row — Launch gate)
claims.claim: "no — never touches PATH"
claims.evidence: cmd/devoid/agent_shim.go, the `claudeGovernanceBypassFlags` docblock states it verbatim: "An IDE-hosted Claude (the VS Code extension, Claude Desktop) never reaches runAgentShim, so it is not covered here." internal/aihooks/transport_route.go:10-23 gives the same reason for existing: "an IDE extension hosts its own runtime and is not launched through our shim".

claims.claim: "yes, asserted into that file"
claims.evidence: internal/aihooks/transport_route.go `mergeTransportRoute`: "It ASSERTS rather than defers to an existing value… a stale value left by an earlier install, a different port, or a hand-edited override would each silently route the IDE around every DeVoid control while the endpoint still reported itself managed." Key `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` (:31), value `http://127.0.0.1:19280/proxy/anthropic` (ProxyBaseURL, :45-54).

claims.claim: "No bypass-flag stripping, no plugin-install gate."
claims.evidence: There are FOUR plugin checkpoints, not one: internal/plugingate/recognize.go:52-63 defines SignalPluginBashTool, SignalPluginSlash, SignalPluginCLI and SignalPluginConfigWrite. Only SignalPluginCLI is the shim-argv path (recognize.go:141 ParseArgv). The other three ride the hook lanes — which the IDE-hosted client runs from the same `~/.claude/settings.json` this row's own Hooks column confirms. So the IDE loses one plugin checkpoint of four, not the gate.
claims.correctedText: | **Claude in an IDE / Desktop** | no — never touches PATH | yes, same settings file | yes, asserted into that file | n/a | **Prompts and traffic covered.** No bypass-flag stripping; three of the four plugin checkpoints still apply through the hooks, but the shim-argv one — a plugin install typed at a terminal the shim never saw — does not. |

claims.docLine: L137 (§3.3, Codex CLI row — Hooks column)
claims.claim: "5 events, 3 gating"
claims.evidence: internal/codexmanaged/hookset.go:92-96 — PreToolUse (Gating:true), UserPromptSubmit (Gating:true), PostToolUse (false), SessionStart (false), PermissionRequest (Gating:true). Five rows, three gating. Corroborated by internal/airuntime/adapters/codex/effects.go:44-50, where deny-prompt / deny-tool / deny-escalation are the three deny effects.

claims.claim: "**Machine lane covered; cooperative hook lane inert.**"
claims.evidence: hookdialect.go:166 now carries two dialect rows. The cooperative lane was measured firing on 0.147.0 (register.json `codex-hook-fires-and-client-honours-deny`, observed:true, 2026-08-27T11:48:30Z — client log "hook: PreToolUse Blocked", DENY_SIDE_EFFECT.txt absent, allow control created its marker, trust-hash negative control made the hook vanish entirely). What still kills the lane is OUR OWN configuration, not the dialect: cmd/devoid/ai_codex_lanes.go:296 and :347 and cmd/devoid/codex_machine_hook_argv.go:24 — the machine baseline's `allow_managed_hooks_only = true` "suppresses the USER-scope hook lane". The proof was taken on a box whose real C:\\ProgramData\\OpenAI\\Codex was EMPTY, and its own evidence says "THIS PROOF DOES NOT COVER A MACHINE-BASELINED ENDPOINT".
claims.correctedText: | **Codex (CLI)** | yes | 5 events, 3 gating — but see below | yes, via a config-persisted provider route | n/a | **Machine lane covered. Cooperative lane fires on 0.144.x and 0.147.x — and only where no machine baseline is present**, because our own `allow_managed_hooks_only` pin suppresses it. |
claims.labelChange: cooperative hook lane inert -> CONDITIONAL (conditions, both required: client version in {0.144.x, 0.147.x}; AND no machine baseline pinning allow_managed_hooks_only=true). PROVEN LIVE on 0.147 in the cooperative scope only.

claims.docLine: L138 (§3.3, Codex desktop / VS Code row)
claims.claim: "The full profile is a proven brick, so five of six admin locks are withheld."
claims.evidence: internal/codexmanaged/requirements.go:313 names them: "withheld admin locks (R1, R2, R3, R4 and R6)". :364 — `var desktopRequirements = []string{R5ProviderRoute, R7HookCoop, R8HookLifecycle}`. Six admin locks R1–R6 (:168-173); only R5 survives into the desktop set. The "proven brick" half gained a second, sharper measurement on 2026-08-27 (register.json, `codex-hook-fires-and-client-honours-deny`): under the full profile codex 0.147 downgrades `--sandbox workspace-write` to read-only on Windows while R2 pins workspace-write and R1 pins approval_policy=never, so the client declines every shell command itself in 0 ms — "rejected: blocked by policy" — and refuses danger-full-access outright.
claims.correctedText: | **Codex desktop / VS Code** | no | cooperative only | provider route only | n/a | **Deliberately degraded.** Five of the six admin locks (R1–R4, R6) are withheld; only the provider route survives. Re-measured 2026-08-27: under the full profile a Codex tool call cannot run on Windows *at all* — 0.147 downgrades `workspace-write` to read-only, so R1+R2 together make the client decline every command in 0 ms before any hook verdict can matter. |

claims.claim: "yes | **none** | **none** | n/a | **Launch-time only.** Once it starts we see nothing."
claims.evidence: Launch gate: cmd/devoid/agent_shim.go `agentShimNames() = {"claude","codex","gemini"}`. Hooks: `git ls-tree -d origin/main internal/airuntime/adapters/` returns exactly two directories, claudecode and codex — there is no Gemini adapter, and internal/aihooks manages only Claude's settings.json. Wire: internal/aiagent/aiagent.go TransportEnvFor — `case AgentTypeGemini: return "", false`, with the comment "no stable base-URL override wired".

claims.claim: "**Inventoried, not intercepted.** Labels exist; no enforcer does."
claims.evidence: An enforcer does exist and it writes into both editors. internal/policybundle/extensions_allowed.go:30-35 targets four editor settings.json files; `desiredExtensionsAllowed` (:39-49) writes the deny-by-default baseline `{"*": false}` under `extensions.allowed` in enforce and audit modes. The same table marks Cursor `Honored: false` and Windsurf `Honored: false` — the struct field is documented at :17 as "whether the host is known to honor extensions.allowed", and a false value emits telemetry that the key may be ignored. Separately, internal/mcpsources/mcpsources.go carries five discovery sources for these editors (cursor user, cursor project, windsurf, cursor-app, windsurf-app), and MCP quarantine physically edits those configs. So it is not that no enforcer exists — it is that the one that exists writes a key those two editors are not known to read.
claims.correctedText:
| **Cursor / Windsurf** | no | no | no | no — neither has a browser surface | **Configs written, nothing honoured.** MCP servers in their configs are discovered and quarantinable, and we write an `extensions.allowed` deny-by-default baseline into both — a control our own table records as **not honoured** by either editor (`extensions_allowed.go:32-34`, `Honored: false`). VS Code and VSCodium are the two hosts marked `Honored: true`. |
| **GitHub Copilot** | no | no | no | yes, on `copilot.microsoft.com` and `github.com/copilot` | **Web chat covered; the IDE extension is not.** |
claims.labelChange: "no enforcer does" -> SHIPS-but-not-honoured. The assignment: policybundle.applyExtensionsAllowedToSettings writes the key; the editorSettings row for cursor/windsurf carries Honored:false.

claims.claim: "**Covered** wherever the extension is installed."
claims.evidence: browser-extension/manifest.json at origin/main: version 0.5.17; content_scripts run at document_start on nine origins, which include chatgpt.com, chat.openai.com, claude.ai, gemini.google.com, copilot.microsoft.com and github.com/copilot — all four clients named in the row. The hedge "wherever installed" is doing real work and is never cashed out: install-scripts/production/install.ps1:3373-3402 runs `browser-guard sync` to pre-stage HKLM ExtensionSettings force-install policies for seven browsers, pointing at the self-hosted feed internal/promptguard/constants.go:122 (`https://installers-prod.s3.eu-north-1.amazonaws.com/extensions/chrome/update.xml`, extension id ifbjklbconaoilidakfmmanclglagfem). That path is best-effort and non-fatal on Windows, and internal/browserinv/browserinv_darwinpolicy.go:31-38 and browserinv_unix.go:45-52 both state the hard limit: stock non-MDM macOS Chrome REFUSES off-store force_installed extensions regardless of delivery, and Linux/macOS have no per-user managed-policy path at all.
claims.correctedText: | **ChatGPT / Claude.ai / Gemini web / Copilot web** | n/a | n/a | n/a | yes | **Covered where the extension actually installs.** Windows: a best-effort HKLM force-install policy across seven browsers, from our own S3 update feed, retried by the daemon every sweep. macOS: stock non-MDM Chrome refuses an off-store force-install however it is delivered — an admin must install the emitted `.mobileconfig`. Linux/macOS per-user installs get no managed-policy path at all. The native-messaging host and the daemon-side controls work regardless; only the automatic *install* needs the profile. |

claims.claim: "We pin exactly one format, matching Codex `0.144.x`."
claims.evidence: internal/codexmanaged/hookdialect.go:166 — `var knownHookTrustDialects = []hookTrustDialect{hookTrustDialect144, hookTrustDialect147}`. Row 1 at :100-104 (`id: "codex-hooktrust-0.144"`, minorPrefixes {"0.144."}); row 2 at :111-115 (`id: "codex-hooktrust-0.147"`, minorPrefixes {"0.147."}). The two rows deliberately share `dialect144Identity` because 0.147 was MEASURED to produce byte-identical digests, and the file says why they are not merged into one "0.14" prefix: "0.145/0.146 sit between them unmeasured. A single row spanning \"0.14\" would silently adopt them."
claims.correctedText: We pin exactly two formats, matching Codex `0.144.x` and `0.147.x`. They are two rows rather than one range on purpose: 0.145 and 0.146 sit between them and were never measured, and a wider prefix would silently adopt them — which is precisely how the old firewall went dead.

claims.claim: "A survey on 2026-08-26 found three Codex builds on one machine — `0.147.0`, `0.149.0-alpha.4.1`, `0.130.0-alpha.5` — **none of them 0.144**."
claims.evidence: internal/codexmanaged/hookdialect.go:130-134 records the same survey verbatim: "The 2026-08-26 survey of this table recorded THREE clients on this machine — codex-cli 0.147.0 (npm global), 0.149.0-alpha.4.1 (the desktop app's runtime), 0.130.0-alpha.5 (its launcher, below MinRuntimeVersion)". Independently reconfirmed on the real-box run of 2026-08-27: the owner's own Codex client is 0.149.0-alpha.4.1.

claims.claim: "On today's shipped clients the cooperative Codex hook does not fire. **INERT.**"
claims.evidence: Two independent disproofs. (1) hookdialect.go:139-160 records the acceptance artefacts for 0.147: `codex app-server` hooks/list returning currentHash = sha256:36c60bf4… byte-equal to the 0.144 golden vector and trustStatus "trusted", plus a live trust-gated `codex exec` with a one-nibble-wrong hash as the negative control. (2) register.json `codex-hook-fires-and-client-honours-deny` is observed:true — the client's own log reads "hook: PreToolUse" / "Command blocked by PreToolUse hook" / "hook: PreToolUse Blocked", the side-effect marker was never created, and removing only the `[hooks.state]` trusted_hash made the same command run. The conclusion the paragraph reaches nonetheless survives *for this machine*, for a different reason: 0.149.0-alpha.4.1 is outside both rows, and hookdialect.go:156-158 lists "STILL UNMEASURED, STILL UNRESOLVABLE: 0.145, 0.146, 0.148 and the 0.149 alpha the desktop app runs."
claims.correctedText: On a 0.144.x or 0.147.x client with no machine baseline, the cooperative Codex hook fires, decides, and the client honours the deny — measured end to end on 0.147 with a trust-hash negative control (§15). It does not fire anywhere else, and "anywhere else" includes the client on the machine this document was written on: the owner's Codex is `0.149.0-alpha.4.1`, outside both rows, and 0.145 / 0.146 / 0.148 / 0.149 remain unmeasured and therefore unresolvable by design. additions.where: §3.3, immediately under the coverage table — a new short paragraph before the Codex caveat
additions.text: **When coverage begins is not when the installer finishes.** On a Windows machine-scope install the MSI does not wire the AI hook lane at all. It registers a per-user scheduled task — `Devoid AI Governance Reconcile`, principal BUILTIN\Users at least privilege, pinned to `<machine root>\bin\devoid-daemon.exe ai reconcile` — whose logon trigger is deliberately delayed one minute so the reconcile does not race the logon storm and the daemon has time to bind its loopback proxy. It then repeats every five minutes, while the real work is throttled to fifteen. So a freshly installed endpoint has no Claude hooks and no asserted transport route for roughly the first minute of the user's session, and if the task fails to register the install still succeeds: registration is strictly best-effort and every outcome is logged and returned. Every 'yes' in the Hooks and Wire columns above is a statement about the steady state, not about minute zero.
additions.evidence: Installers/internal/aiwiretask/aiwiretask.go:144 (TaskName), :150 (TaskArguments = "ai reconcile"), :154 (TaskExeName), :170 (RepeatInterval = "PT5M"), :178 (LogonDelay = "PT1M"); cmd/devoid/ai_wire_user_task.go:41-46 ("STRICTLY BEST-EFFORT… nothing here exits, prints to stdout/stderr, or propagates an error"). omissions.proposedText:
Add to §3.2, after the Surface Access paragraph:

**And one gate outranks the administrator entirely.** Thirty-nine detector classes sit on a *malicious floor* — thirteen destructive-execution classes and eight self-tampering classes pinned at `block`, twelve credential classes pinned at `redact`, four injection-that-acts classes, plus two credential-read tool classes. Since 2026-08-27 the floor is applied as the unconditional first statement of every effective-policy assembly, which is the only way to build a wire payload. An administrator may store a weaker value; the console will show it, the write returns 200, and the endpoint is served the floored value on the next pull. The stored row is not rewritten and a warning names every raise in the server log. This is deliberate — it is what makes the floor unbypassable rather than a property of whichever caller remembered to call it — but it means the sentence 'the customer's administrator sets the policy' in §1 has a named exception, and `destructive-rm` is the one customers will find first (§4).

omissions.what: A clean uninstall leaves 41 files and ~424 MB in C:\ProgramData\devoid\bin, including executables named claude.exe, codex.exe and npm.exe.
omissions.whyItMatters: §3's checkpoint 1 explains that our interception mechanism is byte-copies of our binary wearing other programs' names on PATH. The document never says what happens to them when the product is removed. A customer's security team that finds an unowned `claude.exe` in ProgramData after uninstalling us will treat it as a compromise, not as leftover. The ACL is correct and PATH is cleaned so there is no interception — but the residue is permanent, because the hardening custom action has no uninstall counterpart anywhere in the .wxs set.
omissions.evidence: windows-installer/msi-build/CustomActions.wxs:600-601 — CA_Rollback_HardenShims and CA_HardenShims are both conditioned `(NOT Installed OR REINSTALL) AND NOT REMOVE~="ALL"`. Grepping the three .wxs files (Bundle.wxs, CustomActions.wxs, Product.wxs) for a shim-removal counterpart finds none; the uninstall sequence at :643-656 runs CA_KillProcesses, CA_TeardownMachineState, CA_DeregisterEndpoint and CA_RemoveDaemonTask only. omissions.proposedText:
Add to §3, as a note under the five-checkpoint table (and cross-reference from §14):

**Checkpoint 1 leaves a permanent trace.** The shims are byte-copies of our binary named `claude.exe`, `codex.exe`, `npm.exe` and thirteen others, in `%ProgramData%\devoid\bin`. Measured on a real box on 2026-08-27: a clean uninstall exits 0, restores every user configuration file byte-identically, and leaves 41 files and roughly 424 MB of that directory in place. PATH is cleaned and the directory ACL is correct, so nothing is intercepted afterwards — but nothing removes them either, because the install-time hardening action is conditioned `NOT REMOVE~="ALL"` and has no uninstall counterpart in the WiX set. omissions.what: §4's walkthroughs never show a decision that is neither allowed nor blocked — the hold, the warn dialog, and what the developer does next.
omissions.whyItMatters: All four walkthroughs end in a clean allow or a clean block. The product's most common interactive outcome is neither: a warn becomes an interactive hold on the wire, a hold has a 40-second ceiling and a 30-second dialog, and an unanswered warn on a non-interactive session downgrades to allow — except for a conclusive secret, which becomes a block. A PM reading §4 will not know the product ever asks the human anything, and will not know that an unanswered question resolves *permissively* by default. That is the behaviour a customer will describe as 'it let it through'.
omissions.evidence: §6.1's budget table (hold ceiling 40 s, warn dialog 30 s) and §13.1's row 'A warn with no interactive human → Downgrades to allow — except a conclusive secret, which becomes block' both exist deep in Part II; §4 has no walkthrough for either. cmd/devoid/agent_shim.go threads `interactive := stdinIsTerminal()` into buildAgentEnv and the control headers precisely so the wire lane knows whether a human can answer.
omissions.proposedText:
Add a fourth-and-a-half walkthrough:

**A developer's prompt trips a warn, and nobody is at the keyboard.** A warn is not a soft block — on the wire it becomes an interactive hold, released only by a single-use, digest-bound allow-once. The developer gets 30 seconds to answer in a dialog, inside a 40-second hold ceiling, inside the host's 60-second hook timeout. If the session is not interactive — a CI job, an agent running headless, a piped stdin — there is nobody to ask, and the warn **downgrades to allow**. The single exception is a conclusive secret, which becomes a block instead. So the same policy produces opposite outcomes depending on whether a terminal is attached, and the permissive one is the default.

reorganisation:
Four structural changes, in priority order.

1. **§3.3 needs a fifth column and two split rows.** The table has four columns for a five-checkpoint model, and the missing column — the machine lane — is the only one that reaches Cursor, Windsurf and Gemini's MCP configuration. Add a "Machine lane" column.
